CALIFORNIA STATUTORY WILL — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Los Angeles

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the California statutory will created by California Probate Code Section 6200 et seq. -- a will form that the California Legislature drafted and set out verbatim in the statute itself -- for Jane Doe, a resident of Los Angeles County, California, who may be considering whether to use it. It states facts about this specific form under California law generally. It does not determine whether this form fits Jane Doe's particular estate, and it does not advise on whether to adopt it.

WHAT A CALIFORNIA STATUTORY WILL IS
California law recognizes one specific, codified will form: the California statutory will. Its content is fixed by the Probate Code itself, in Section 6240, rather than being freely drafted the way a custom will is. The statute defines a "testator," for purposes of this specific instrument, as a person choosing to adopt a California statutory will. There is only one California statutory will, and it consists of the text of the Section 6240 form (apart from that section's introductory questions and answers), together -- by reference -- with the statute's own definitions and rules of construction, whichever property disposition clauses the testator selects on the form, and a fixed set of mandatory clauses set out elsewhere in the statute. If Jane Doe were to adopt this form, Jane Doe would be adopting this same fixed instrument, not a custom-drafted one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Unless the provision or context clearly requires otherwise, these definitions and rules of construction govern the construction of this chapter."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6200 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, definitions and rules of construction govern this chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6200.)
  "“Testator” means a person choosing to adopt a California statutory will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6201 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, definition of "testator" for the statutory will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6201.)
  "(a) There is only one California statutory will.  (b) The California statutory will includes all of the following:  (1) The contents of the California statutory will form set out in Section 6240, excluding the questions and answers at the beginning of the California statutory will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6223(a)-(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, there is only one California statutory will and what it includes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6223.)
  Known gap: Three separate statutory sections are cited here (Section 6200, Section 6201, and Section 6223), not subdivisions of a single section; Section 6223 itself has its own subdivisions (a) and (b)(1), quoted together below because they directly define what the statutory will is and what it includes. This clause does not reproduce the operative fill-in-the-blank text of the Section 6240 form itself: the version of Section 6240 published by the Legislature's own online law database (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) does not carry that text. In its place, the fetched page states, verbatim: "NOTICE OF INCOMPLETE TEXT: The California Statutory Will appears in the hard-copy publication of the chaptered bill. See Sec. 88, Chapter 50 (pp. 77-82), Statutes of 2016." So the actual paragraph-and-blank text of the form is not available from this source and is not quoted or reproduced anywhere in this corpus; a separate drafting clause in this document describes the form's structure from the introductory material that is published, without presenting that description as the form's own text.

HOW A STATUTORY WILL MUST BE EXECUTED
The statutory will is not executed under the same statute that governs a custom-drafted will; the Probate Code sets a separate, self-contained execution rule for it. Any individual of sound mind and over the age of 18 -- which would include Jane Doe, if that description applies -- may execute a California statutory will. To execute it, the testator completes the form's blanks and signs the will, and each witness must observe the testator's signing and sign the witness's own name in the testator's presence. A completed attestation clause signed by two or more witnesses satisfies the separate Probate Code requirement for proving a witnessed will at probate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any individual of sound mind and over the age of 18 may execute a California statutory will under the provisions of this chapter."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6220 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, who may execute a California statutory will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6220.)
  "A California statutory will shall be executed only as follows: (a) The testator shall complete the appropriate blanks and shall sign the will. (b) Each witness shall observe the testator’s signing and each witness shall sign his or her name in the presence of the testator."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6221 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, execution requirements specific to the statutory will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6221.)
  "The execution of the attestation clause provided in the California statutory will by two or more witnesses satisfies Section 8220."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6222 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, attestation clause satisfies the proof-at-probate requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6222.)
  Known gap: Three separate sections are cited (Section 6220, Section 6221, and Section 6222), not subdivisions of one section. Section 6221's text, as quoted, requires each witness to observe the testator's signing and sign in the testator's presence, but -- unlike the general will-execution statute already cited elsewhere in this corpus (Cal. Prob. Code Section 6110(c)(1), which expressly requires the witnesses to be present at the same time as each other) -- Section 6221's text does not itself state whether the two witnesses must be present at the same time as one another; this clause does not resolve that difference and does not assume Section 6110's simultaneous-presence requirement carries over. Section 6222 cross-references Section 8220 of the Probate Code (a proof-of-will-at-probate provision) rather than restating its text; Section 8220 was not independently fetched or verified for this clause, and only the fact of the cross-reference is stated. A separate clause in this document covers Section 6226(c), which provides an additional, "notwithstanding Section 6110," path to validating a defectively executed statutory will.

WHAT THE STATUTORY WILL FORM STATES IT IS NOT DESIGNED FOR
The statutory will form's own text places real limits on what it is designed to do. It states that it is a simple will, not designed to reduce death taxes or other taxes, and that a person should talk to a lawyer about tax planning instead, especially if the person's assets will be worth more than $600,000 (or the amount currently excluded from federal estate tax at death), the person owns business-related assets, wants to create a trust fund for children's education or other purposes, owns assets in another state, wants to disinherit a spouse, domestic partner, or descendants, or has valuable pension or profit-sharing plan interests. The same text states that a person completing the form may only fill in its blanks -- adding or crossing out any other words risks making the will invalid or having the added or crossed-out words disregarded by a court -- and, separately, states that trusts generally are "too complicated to be used in this Statutory Will."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "8. Are there any reasons why I should NOT use this Statutory Will?  Yes. This is a simple Will. It is not designed to reduce death taxes or other taxes. Talk to a lawyer to do tax planning, especially if (i) your assets will be worth more than $600,000 or the current amount excluded from estate tax under federal law at your death, (ii) you own business-related assets, (iii) you want to create a trust fund for your children’s education or other purposes, (iv) you own assets in some other state, (v) you want to disinherit your spouse, domestic partner, or descendants, or (vi) you have valuable interests in pension or profit-sharing plans. You should talk to a lawyer who
				knows about estate planning if this Will does not meet your needs."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6240 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, statutory will form's own caution against tax planning, business assets, trusts, out-of-state assets, disinheriting a spouse or partner or descendants, and pension interests (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6240.)
  "9. May I add or cross out any words on this Will?  No. If you do, the Will may be invalid or the court may ignore the crossed out or added words. You may only fill in the blanks. You may amend this Will by a separate document (called a codicil). Talk to a lawyer if you want to do something with your assets which is not allowed in this form."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6240 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, statutory will form's own instruction that only the blanks may be filled in (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6240.)
  "20. What is a trust?  There are many kinds of trusts, including trusts created by Wills (called “testamentary trusts”) and trusts created during your lifetime (called “revocable living trusts”). Both kinds of trusts are long-term arrangements
				in which a manager (called a “trustee”) invests and manages assets for someone (called a “beneficiary”) on the terms you specify. Trusts are too complicated to be used in this Statutory Will. You should see a lawyer if you want to create a trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6240 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, statutory will form's own statement that trusts are too complicated for this form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6240.)
  Known gap: All three quotes below come from the same statutory section, Section 6240 -- specifically from the numbered questions-and-answers text (questions 8, 9, and 20) that the statute places before the form itself. Section 6223(b)(1), quoted in another clause in this document, expressly excludes that questions-and-answers text from the definition of "the California statutory will" -- meaning this limitations text is explanatory material the Legislature placed in the statute, not itself an operative clause of the will. The $600,000 figure is the fixed number written into the statute; the statute's own text ties the actual test to whichever figure is "the current amount excluded from estate tax under federal law" at the testator's death, which is a materially larger, adjusting figure today, so the $600,000 number by itself is not a current test. This clause does not cover every scenario the questions-and-answers text flags as a reason not to use the form (for example, its separate caution about stepchildren and foster children who have not been adopted).

EFFECT OF AN INCOMPLETELY OR IMPROPERLY COMPLETED STATUTORY WILL
The statute directly addresses what happens when the form's property disposition clauses are selected incorrectly or the form is altered outside its instructions. If more than one of certain alternative disposition clauses is selected where the form calls for a single choice, no gift is made under that clause; and if the form's residuary-estate clause has more than one option selected, or none, the residuary estate instead passes to the testator's heirs at law, determined as though the testator had not made a will. Separately, any addition to or deletion from the statutory will form, made other than by following the form's own instructions, is given effect only if clear and convincing evidence shows it would carry out the testator's clear intent; absent such a showing, a court may either disregard the addition or deletion or find that all or part of the will is invalid, whichever better matches the testator's intent. Notwithstanding the general will-execution statute that otherwise governs, a document executed on the statutory will form can still be held valid as a will despite a defect if clear and convincing evidence establishes that the testator signed the form, that the testator knew of and approved its contents and intended it to have testamentary effect, and that the testamentary intent reflected in the document is clear.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If more than one property disposition clause appearing in paragraphs 2 or 3 of a California statutory will is selected, no gift is made. If more than one property disposition clause in paragraph 5 of a California statutory will form is selected, or if none is selected, the residuary estate of a testator who signs a California statutory will shall be distributed to the testator’s heirs as if the testator did not make a will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6224 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, effect of selecting more than one, or no, disposition clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6224.)
  "Any additions to or deletions from the California statutory will on the face of the California statutory will form, other than in accordance with the instructions, shall be given effect only where clear and convincing evidence shows that they would effectuate the clear intent of the testator.  In the absence of such a showing, the court either may determine that the addition or deletion is ineffective and shall be disregarded, or may determine that all or a portion of the California statutory will is invalid, whichever is more likely to be consistent with the intent of the testator."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6226(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, effect of additions to or deletions from the statutory will form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6226.)
  "Notwithstanding Section 6110, a document executed on a California statutory will form is valid as a will if all of the following requirements are shown to be satisfied by clear and convincing evidence:  (1) The form is signed by the testator.  (2) The court is satisfied that the testator knew and approved of the contents of the will and intended it to have testamentary effect.  (3) The testamentary intent of the maker as reflected in the document is clear."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6226(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, validating a defectively executed statutory will notwithstanding Section 6110 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6226.)
  Known gap: Section 6224 and Section 6226 are two separate sections; Section 6226(b) and Section 6226(c), both quoted below, are two subdivisions of that same section. Section 6226(c)'s cross-reference to "Section 6110" is to the general will-execution statute already cited elsewhere in this corpus, in the Last Will and Testament document's execution-requirements clause; this clause states only that Section 6226(c) operates notwithstanding Section 6110, and does not restate Section 6110's text here. This clause does not cover Section 6226(a) (the general statement that a statutory will may be revoked or amended by codicil like other wills).

EFFECT OF A LATER DIVORCE OR DISSOLUTION ON A STATUTORY WILL
As with wills generally, a later dissolution or annulment of the testator's marriage, or termination of the testator's registered domestic partnership, has an automatic effect on a previously executed California statutory will: it revokes any disposition of property the will made to the former spouse or partner, and any nomination of the former spouse or partner as executor, trustee, guardian, or custodian. If the testator later remarries that same former spouse, or re-enters a registered domestic partnership with that same former partner, the revoked disposition or nomination is revived.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If after executing a California statutory will the testator’s marriage is dissolved or annulled, or the testator’s registered domestic partnership is terminated, the dissolution, annulment, or termination revokes any disposition of property made by the will to the former spouse and any nomination of the former spouse as executor, trustee, guardian, or custodian made by the will. If any disposition or nomination is revoked solely by this section, it is revived by the testator’s remarriage to, or entry into a subsequent registered domestic partnership with, the former spouse."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6227(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, revocation of dispositions and nominations to a former spouse or partner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6227.)
  Known gap: This is Cal. Prob. Code Section 6227(a) -- a provision written specifically for the statutory will, in the same chapter of the Probate Code as the rest of this document's citations. It runs in parallel to, but is a textually separate statute from, Cal. Prob. Code Section 6122, the general will's divorce-revocation rule already cited elsewhere in this corpus (the Last Will and Testament document's will_revocation_by_divorce clause); this clause does not independently verify Section 6122's text or confirm the two provisions are worded identically. This clause covers only subdivision (a); it does not cover subdivisions (b) through (d), which address how the revoked property passes, define "dissolution or annulment" for this purpose, and carve out dissolutions or annulments finalized before January 1, 1985.

STRUCTURE OF THE STATUTORY WILL FORM (INFORMATIONAL ONLY)
This is a description of the California statutory will form's structure, drawn from the introductory questions-and-answers and instructions the Legislature placed in Probate Code Section 6240 -- it is not the form itself, and completing it is not the same as completing a California statutory will. As that introductory material describes it: the form must be dated and signed by the testator, and signed by two witnesses who follow the notice to witnesses printed on the form; the testator fills in blanks to name an executor (and may name an alternate) and to say whether the executor must post a bond; the testator fills in blanks to select property disposition clauses for specific gifts and for the residuary estate, choosing among the alternatives the form provides; and, if the testator has children under 18, the testator may fill in blanks to nominate a guardian (and an alternate) and, separately, to name a custodian to manage a minor's or young adult's assets under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. The form's introductory material states that a person should not add words to the form or cross words out, beyond filling in the blanks it provides.

CERTIFICATION OF UNDERSTANDING
I certify that I have read this information sheet on the California statutory will under California Probate Code Section 6200 et seq., including its execution requirements, the limitations its own text states, and the effect of an incompletely or improperly completed form, and that this sheet states facts about California law generally rather than advising me on whether to use this particular form for my own estate.

Signed: _______________________ Date: January 1, 2026
At: Los Angeles, California

citations.cite: California Probate Code, revocation of dispositions and nominations to a former spouse or partner
citations.quote: If after executing a California statutory will the testator’s marriage is dissolved or annulled, or the testator’s registered domestic partnership is terminated, the dissolution, annulment, or termination revokes any disposition of property made by the will to the former spouse and any nomination of the former spouse as executor, trustee, guardian, or custodian made by the will. If any disposition or nomination is revoked solely by this section, it is revived by the testator’s remarriage to, or entry into a subsequent registered domestic partnership with, the former spouse.

expectedJSON.gap: This is Cal. Prob. Code Section 6227(a) -- a provision written specifically for the statutory will, in the same chapter of the Probate Code as the rest of this document's citations. It runs in parallel to, but is a textually separate statute from, Cal. Prob. Code Section 6122, the general will's divorce-revocation rule already cited elsewhere in this corpus (the Last Will and Testament document's will_revocation_by_divorce clause); this clause does not independently verify Section 6122's text or confirm the two provisions are worded identically. This clause covers only subdivision (a); it does not cover subdivisions (b) through (d), which address how the revoked property passes, define "dissolution or annulment" for this purpose, and carve out dissolutions or annulments finalized before January 1, 1985.

expectedJSON.body: This is a description of the California statutory will form's structure, drawn from the introductory questions-and-answers and instructions the Legislature placed in Probate Code Section 6240 -- it is not the form itself, and completing it is not the same as completing a California statutory will. As that introductory material describes it: the form must be dated and signed by the testator, and signed by two witnesses who follow the notice to witnesses printed on the form; the testator fills in blanks to name an executor (and may name an alternate) and to say whether the executor must post a bond; the testator fills in blanks to select property disposition clauses for specific gifts and for the residuary estate, choosing among the alternatives the form provides; and, if the testator has children under 18, the testator may fill in blanks to nominate a guardian (and an alternate) and, separately, to name a custodian to manage a minor's or young adult's assets under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. The form's introductory material states that a person should not add words to the form or cross words out, beyond filling in the blanks it provides.
